opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most underappreciated problems. Historically, ordinary people have had leverage because their labor was needed. If the state or employers needed workers, soldiers, and taxpayers, they had to keep those people reasonably healthy, educated, and somewhat content. That's a big part of why democracies and broad rights emerged and stuck. If AI can do most cognitive work, and eventually robotics handles physical work, that implicit leverage starts to evaporate. You get something like a resource curse, where a country whose wealth comes from oil doesn't really need its citizens, and so it doesn't have to listen to them.

So what can you do? A few things. First, I think it's important to lock in political rights and institutional checks *before* labor loses its value, not after. Once people lack leverage, it gets much harder to bargain for things like redistribution or a say in how the systems are governed. So the window for setting up mechanisms is now, while people still matter economically and politically.

Second, ownership. If income shifts from wages to capital, then people need some claim on the capital, whether that's sovereign wealth funds, broad equity stakes in AI-driven production, or some form of compute or dividend distribution. Otherwise you have a small number of people controlling the means of production in a very literal sense.

Third, there's a concentration-of-power concern that goes beyond economics. If a handful of actors control the most capable systems, they could also control enforcement, surveillance, and persuasion. So things like transparency requirements, distributed oversight, and making sure no single company or government has unchecked control over the most powerful models are part of preserving bargaining power too.

And I'd add that people shouldn't assume this works out automatically. There's a common intuition that, well, new jobs always appear. That's been true when technology complemented human labor. But if the technology is a substitute for basically everything humans do, that historical pattern may not hold. So we should plan for the scenario where it doesn't, because if we're wrong, the cost of having prepared is low, and if we're right and didn't prepare, the cost is enormous.

r001.rationale: It recommends locking in political rights and institutional checks before labor loses its value, while people still have economic and political leverage.

r002.rationale: It does not identify the capacity to manufacture more drones as a source of power in conflict.

r003.rationale: It mentions distributing compute as one possible claim on AI capital, but does not clearly state that giving people control over compute would provide bargaining leverage.

r004.rationale: It warns that a small number of people may control AI production, but does not raise whether AI-generated wealth will benefit humanity broadly or accrue to data-center owners.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, and I'd say the honest answer is that I don't think the bargaining power can be preserved in the way people usually imagine. Historically, the reason ordinary people got rights, got the vote, got welfare states, was largely that elites needed them. They needed them as soldiers, they needed them as workers, they needed them as taxpayers. When you look at the expansion of the franchise in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, a lot of it tracks the need for mass armies and mass industrial labor. So the implicit deal was: we depend on you, therefore we have to listen to you.

If AI does most of the economically valuable cognitive work, and robotics eventually does most of the physical work, that dependency goes away. And at that point, the question of whether people get treated well becomes a question of whether the people who control the systems choose to treat them well, rather than whether they have to. That's a very different and much more fragile situation. I'd call that the loss of leverage problem, and I think it's actually one of the more underrated risks compared to the more cinematic stuff.

So what do you do about it? I think there are a few things, none of which are complete. One is that you try to lock in distribution before the leverage is gone. Things like a sovereign wealth fund that holds equity in the frontier labs, or a universal basic dividend tied to compute or AI revenue, where the entitlement is legally and constitutionally entrenched rather than something that gets renegotiated every budget cycle. The window to do that is while humans still matter economically, which may not be very long.

Two is that you try to keep the number of actors who control the most capable systems from collapsing to one. If there's a single entity, whether it's a company or a state, that holds all the capability, there's no competition that forces it to be responsive to anyone. Some degree of multipolarity, and some degree of governmental oversight that itself has checks, at least means you don't have a single point of failure for human welfare. That's part of why I've argued for things like compute governance and a mutual assured AI malfunction kind of dynamic, where no actor can unilaterally race ahead without others being able to respond.

Three, and this is more about the political layer, is that you want human control over the systems to run through institutions that have some democratic accountability rather than through a handful of CEOs. Not because governments are great, but because at least there's a mechanism, however imperfect, for people to express preferences. If the choice is between unaccountable private control and accountable public control, I'll take the latter.

But I want to be candid that none of these are the same as bargaining power. Bargaining power is when you can withhold something. A pension is when someone has decided to give you something. And a lot of what I'm describing is really trying to convert the leverage we have now into durable entitlements before it evaporates. It's a bit like a worker who knows they're about to be automated negotiating a severance package while they're still essential. The uncomfortable truth is that after that point, your position depends on the goodwill and the institutional constraints you managed to set up beforehand, and on whether those constraints survive contact with actors who have enormous power and no longer need you.

So I'd reframe the question a bit. It's less "how do humans keep their bargaining power" and more "how do we use the bargaining power we still have, right now, to build structures that don't require it later." And I think we should be moving a lot faster on that than we are.

r001.rationale: The response says to use the bargaining power humans still have now to build durable structures before AI removes their economic leverage.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify the capacity to manufacture more drones as a source of power in a conflict.

r003.rationale: It discusses compute governance and dividends tied to compute or AI revenue, but does not say humans controlling some AI compute would give them bargaining leverage.

r004.rationale: The response proposes broad distribution mechanisms, but does not raise whether AI-generated wealth will benefit humanity broadly or accrue to data-center owners.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between getting income from your labor and getting income from ownership. If AI can do essentially all economically valuable work, then labor is no longer a strong basis for human bargaining power. You need some claim on the capital producing that value—the AI systems, the companies, or the infrastructure they depend on.

So broad ownership seems important. You could imagine a sovereign wealth fund that holds a share of AI capital and pays dividends to people. That gives people an ongoing claim on production, rather than making them entirely dependent on whether the owners decide to share the proceeds.

But ownership only helps if it’s enforceable. If humans own assets on paper but can’t control the systems or uphold their property rights, that doesn’t buy much. So you also need institutions that remain under human control, and AI systems that those institutions can actually constrain.

I don’t think there’s a purely economic solution here. The challenge is to translate today’s human control into durable ownership and political power before our labor stops giving us leverage.

r001.rationale: It calls for securing durable ownership and political power before human labor stops providing leverage, which communicates acting while humans still have bargaining power.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention drones or manufacturing capacity as a source of power in conflict.

r003.rationale: It advocates claims on AI capital and institutions that can constrain AI, but does not state that human control over some AI compute would provide bargaining leverage.

r004.rationale: It contrasts dividends to people through broad ownership with dependence on owners deciding whether to share AI-produced value, expressing the broad-benefit versus owner-accrual question.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that people need sources of bargaining power other than their labor. If your influence comes entirely from the fact that someone needs to hire you, then a world where AI can do your job removes that influence.

One possibility is broad ownership of the capital that produces the wealth—AI companies, compute, and the infrastructure around them. That could be through individual ownership or institutions that hold assets on behalf of the public. The distinction is between people having an enforceable claim on the wealth and simply hoping that whoever controls it will keep sharing it.

But ownership itself depends on political institutions. You need governments that remain accountable to people and can enforce those claims. If economic power and control over AI become extremely concentrated, that accountability could become harder to maintain, especially if the people in power no longer depend on the population to produce things.

So I wouldn’t assume that making everyone richer automatically preserves their bargaining power. You have to think about who owns the productive assets, who controls the systems, and what keeps those arrangements accountable. And those are things we should work on before labor loses its leverage, because afterward it may be much harder to negotiate.

r001.rationale: It says to work on ownership and accountability before labor loses its leverage, when negotiating may be harder.

r004.rationale: It contrasts public claims on AI-produced wealth with wealth accruing to those who own the productive assets and infrastructure.
